result.summary: Agesilaus becomes king and leads a Spartan expedition against Persia, but is insulted by Thebans at Aulis. After victories in Asia, the Persian satrap Tithraustes funds enemies in Greece, a war starts, and Agesilaus is recalled and wins at Coronea.

scenes.title: Preparing the Asian expedition
scenes.summary: The Lacedaemonians decide to attack Artaxerxes, and Agesilaus seeks allies. Corinth, Athens and Thebes hold back.
scenes.stakes: Agesilaus needs allies for a risky war against the Persian king.

scenes.title: Sacrifice at Aulis
scenes.summary: Agesilaus sacrifices at Aulis in imitation of Agamemnon, but Thebans attack and drive him out. He sails on to Asia.
scenes.stakes: His sacrifice and his honour are insulted before the campaign begins.

scenes.title: Victory near Sardis
scenes.summary: Agesilaus defeats Tissaphernes near the Hermus and is made fleet commander, appointing Pisander.
scenes.stakes: Facing the largest Persian army since Xerxes.

place.name: Plain of the Hermus, near Sardis

scenes.title: Persian gold stirs Greece
scenes.summary: Tithraustes replaces the executed Tissaphernes and bribes Greek politicians. A Locrian-Phocian quarrel leads Sparta to declare war on Thebes.
scenes.stakes: Sparta faces war at home that threatens its Asian campaign.

scenes.title: Agesilaus returns; Coronea
scenes.summary: The Corinthian war recalls Agesilaus, who crosses the Hellespont, fights through Thessaly and wins at Coronea, sparing the refugees in Athene's temple.
scenes.stakes: He is wounded and must fight his way home through hostile territory.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' typical remark that divine envy blocked Agesilaus's success.

analysis.text: Agesilaus models himself on Agamemnon, but his ambition is undone by Greek rivalries and Persian gold.
The passage reflects the early 390s BC, when Persia used bribery to divide Greek states and trigger the Corinthian War.

fun_facts.text: Agamemnon's sacrifice at Aulis before Troy was the mythic model Agesilaus deliberately imitated.

language_notes.text: "Except at Argos and outside the Isthmus" means all Greeks of the Peloponnese other than the Argives, and those living beyond the Isthmus of Corinth, were invited.
A temple burning was read as a sign of divine displeasure; the Corinthians took the fire as a warning against the campaign.
Platæa's capture (427 BC) ended with the Spartan execution of its surviving garrison; Aristomenidas had helped judge them, so Theban friendship was expected.
"Cried off" is colloquial: they withdrew from the commitment and refused to join.
At Aulis, Agamemnon's fleet gathered before Troy and he sacrificed to Artemis to gain favourable winds; Agesilaus deliberately imitates this.
The thigh-bones were the portion burned for the gods; scattering them off the altar ruined the rite.
"Grudged" reflects the Greek idea of divine envy (phthonos), whereby gods resent excessive human success.
"Longheaded" is an old idiom for shrewd, far-sighted; it describes Tithraustes' cunning, not his physical appearance.
A satrapy was a province of the Persian empire, governed by a satrap on behalf of the king.
"With Argive proclivities" means Corinthians favouring Argos, an inclination that made them open to Persian money against Sparta.
"Inveighed against" means spoke bitterly in accusation of.
Refers to Thebans disrupting Agesilaus' sacrifice at Aulis before his Asian campaign, scattering the offerings and treating the king's rite with contempt.
The author refers back to his earlier account of the Spartan king Pausanias, and of Lysander's death at Haliartus in Boeotia.

context_notes.text: Lysander was the Spartan admiral who won the Peloponnesian War; Cyrus the Younger funded Sparta's fleet against Athens.
Conon, an Athenian admiral, took service with the Persian king, so Athens had reason to avoid fighting him.
Sardis was the old Lydian capital, famed for wealth; Susa was the Persian royal capital.
Tissaphernes was the Persian satrap (provincial governor) in western Asia Minor; the Hermus is the river flowing past Sardis.
Pisander was Agesilaus' brother-in-law; he later died commanding the Spartan fleet at Cnidus in 394 BC.
Artaxerxes II was king of Persia. Tissaphernes had been a major Persian commander against the Greeks in Asia Minor.
The Corinthian war (395–387 BC) pitted Sparta against Thebes, Athens, Corinth and Argos, partly financed by Persian money.
Athene Itonia was a goddess worshipped at a Boeotian sanctuary near Coronea; violating suppliants there would have been sacrilege.

literary_notes.text: Agesilaus measures himself against Agamemnon, casting Persia as a greater Troy and framing the expedition as a heroic epic.
The grief over the unfinished sacrifice hints that the campaign will not end as hoped.
This brief closing remark darkens a tale of success, anticipating Agesilaus' later recall and frustrated ambitions.
Persia wins the war not by arms but by gold sent to Greek politicians, who ruin their own country's unity.
Agesilaus is shown as pious: though wounded, he respects the sanctuary and spares his defeated enemies.
